steps.say: Modern endoscopes see so well because of a clever lens swap. The Hopkins system replaces curved glass lenses with long glass rods divided by thin air gaps. Rods carry far more light and resolve finer detail. That is why a slim rigid cystoscope still shows a bright sharp panorama of the bladder lining.
steps.tx: See through glass rods instead of lenses: the **rigid endoscope** (rigid telescope) works on the **Hopkins rod lens system** (**rod lens optics**, glass rod train) in which long glass rods separated by thin air spaces replace traditional curved lenses. The rods carry far more **light transmission** (brightness throughput) with sharper **resolution** (image clarity), so slim cystoscopes still deliver bright panoramic views of the bladder wall.

vis.alt: Rigid laparoscopic telescope used for Hopkins rod lens endoscopy.
vis.caption: Laparoscopic telescope: Hopkins rod lens optics carry bright sharp views down slim barrels. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: Each bend of the bladder needs its own viewing angle. A zero degree scope looks straight ahead for routine checks and ureter work. The thirty degree lens is the everyday inspector. Seventy degrees reaches the side wall and dome, while one hundred twenty degrees looks back at the bladder neck. The surgeon spins the light post to sweep the view without shifting the sheath.
steps.tx: Pick among the four telescope viewing angles for the address: **0 degree** (**straight ahead**, forward view) scopes suit diagnostic cystoscopy and ureterorenoscopy, the **30 degree** (**standard oblique**, angled view) lens is the workhorse for inspection, **70 degree** (**lateral view**, side view) lenses expose the lateral wall and dome, and **120 degree** (**retrograde view**, backward view) lenses inspect the bladder neck from below. Rotating the light post steers the field without moving the sheath.

steps.say: Monopolar current goes through the whole patient to reach its pad. The loop cuts at the tip while a large plate on the skin collects the current. Any leak along the way can burn bowel far from the camera view. Cracked insulation and metal to metal contact are the classic culprits, so every sheath gets checked before switching on.
steps.tx: Complete the circuit through the patient: **monopolar electrosurgery** (**single electrode diathermy**) drives current from the loop through tissue to a dispersive **return electrode pad** (patient plate) stuck on skin. The current must travel the body, so **direct coupling** (stray current to metal) or insulation failure can burn bowel unseen outside the visual field, demanding intact sheaths and isolated instruments.

steps.say: Bipolar instruments keep electricity local. Both electrodes sit on the tip, so current crosses only the tissue between them. No pad on the patient is needed. Saline replaces glycine as the irrigant, which removes the dilutional sodium crash of classic TUR syndrome. That pairing makes bipolar the modern standard for prostate resection.
steps.tx: Keep the current at the tip: **bipolar electrosurgery** (**twin electrode diathermy**) mounts active and return electrodes together on the instrument tip, so current crosses only gripped tissue and no **ground pad** (patient plate) is needed. Working in conductive **saline** (salt water irrigant) instead of glycine removes **TUR syndrome** (dilutional hyponatraemia) risk, which is why bipolar loops rule modern resection.

Glycine irrigant risks TUR syndrome dilution

steps.say: Keyhole surgery needs a gas filled working dome. Carbon dioxide wins because blood dissolves it fast and the lungs blow it off, plus it cannot catch fire near diathermy. Pressure is held between twelve and fifteen millimetres of mercury. Less pressure loses the view, while more pressure chokes veins and starves kidneys of blood.
steps.tx: Fill the belly with **carbon dioxide** (**CO2**, insufflation gas): high blood **solubility** (dissolving power), non flammability, and rapid lung clearance make it the insufflation gas of choice. Hold **intra abdominal pressure** (belly pressure) at **12 to 15 mmHg** (twelve to fifteen millimetres of mercury): lower pressures collapse the view while higher pressures squeeze venous return and renal perfusion.

rows: Carbon dioxide, soluble and non flammable
Venous return and renal flow squeezed

steps.say: Long gas filled operations acidify the blood from absorbed carbon dioxide. The belly lining drinks in CO2 across hours of surgery. Rising arterial gas with falling pH is hypercarbia with respiratory acidosis. The anaesthetist responds with faster deeper breathing on the ventilator that clears the gas through the lungs.
steps.tx: Blame absorbed gas for acid blood: peritoneal absorption of **CO2** (gas uptake) during long laparoscopy raises arterial carbon dioxide as **hypercarbia** (high CO2) with **respiratory acidosis** (acid blood pH). The fix belongs to the anaesthetist, who raises **minute ventilation** (breaths per minute times volume) to blow off the load, so falling pH with rising end tidal CO2 means ventilate more, not desufflate first.

steps.say: The first port is the most dangerous stab of laparoscopy. The Hasson technique cuts down to the peritoneum under direct vision and docks a blunt port openly. No blind needle goes in first. Previous abdominal surgery makes this the default, because old scars plaster bowel exactly where a blind needle would strike.
steps.tx: Open the first port under vision: the **Hasson open technique** (open cutdown access) gives **direct visual access** (seen layers, no blind stab) while seating a blunt trocar, skipping blind **Veress needle** (blind insufflation needle) puncture entirely. Choose it after prior **abdominal surgery** (previous operations) where adhesions glue bowel to the wall, since blind stabs there lacerate mesentery and gut.

rows: Cut down to peritoneum under vision

steps.say: Some instruments cut with sound instead of sparks. Ultrasonic shears keep vibrating over fifty five thousand times a second, melting protein into a seal. They keep sealing vessels up to five millimetres wide. Heat creeps less than a millimetre sideways, so nearby nerves and the ureter stay safe while the target vessel seals.
steps.tx: Shake vessels sealed: **ultrasonic shears** (**Harmonic scalpel**, vibrating blades) oscillate longitudinally at **55.5 kHz** (fifty five point five kilohertz) to denature protein and weld vessels up to **5 mm** (five millimetres) shut. **Lateral thermal spread** (sideways heat damage) stays under **1 mm** (one millimetre), so nerves and ureters beside the jaws survive while the target seals bloodlessly.
